sentence: "It was a most enjoyable evening." What does "a most enjoyable evening" mean here?
setupText: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
taskText: "It was a most enjoyable evening." What does "a most enjoyable evening" mean here?
text: Choose the meaning of the article phrase. "It was a most enjoyable evening." What does "a most enjoyable evening" mean here?
options: The most enjoyable evening out of every evening compared
An evening enjoyed by most of the guests
A very enjoyable evening, without an explicit ranking
An evening that was enjoyable for most of its duration
answer: A very enjoyable evening, without an explicit ranking
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-421:A most as an intensifier versus the most as a ranking
explanation: In this formal expression, "a most enjoyable" means "a very enjoyable". "The most enjoyable" would identify the top evening in a comparison.

rationales.The most enjoyable evening out of every: That is the normal ranking meaning of "the most enjoyable evening", not the intensifying use with "a".
rationales.A very enjoyable evening, without an exp: The indefinite article supports the formal intensifier meaning of most.
rationales.An evening enjoyed by most of the guests: "Most" modifies enjoyable here; it does not count the guests.
rationales.An evening that was enjoyable for most o: Nothing in the article phrase divides the evening into enjoyable and unenjoyable periods.

sentence: "We still have a few seats, so you can join us." Why does "a few" fit the invitation?
setupText: Choose the interpretation that preserves the writer's emphasis.
taskText: "We still have a few seats, so you can join us." Why does "a few" fit the invitation?
text: Choose the interpretation that preserves the writer's emphasis. "We still have a few seats, so you can join us." Why does "a few" fit the invitation?
options: It emphasises that almost no seats remain and therefore discourages attendance
It identifies seats already reserved for the listener
It presents the small number of remaining seats positively as available
It says the speaker cannot estimate whether any seats remain
answer: It presents the small number of remaining seats positively as available
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-422:Positive orientation created by a in a few
explanation: "A few" means some, though not many. That positive orientation supports "you can join us". Bare "few" would emphasise scarcity instead.

rationales.It presents the small number of remainin: The article changes the orientation towards the seats that do remain, which supports the invitation.
rationales.It emphasises that almost no seats remai: That interpretation is closer to bare "few" and conflicts with the invitation.
rationales.It identifies seats already reserved for: "A few" indicates an unspecified number; it does not identify reserved seats.
rationales.It says the speaker cannot estimate whet: The phrase asserts that some seats remain, though it does not give an exact count.

sentence: The guide cancels the climb because the group has almost no experience. Which explanation keeps that emphasis?
setupText: Choose the wording that supports the stated reason for cancelling.
taskText: The guide cancels the climb because the group has almost no experience. Which explanation keeps that emphasis?
text: Choose the wording that supports the stated reason for cancelling. The guide cancels the climb because the group has almost no experience. Which explanation keeps that emphasis?
options: We have little experience of climbing.
We have a little experience of climbing.
We have a little of the experience of climbing.
We have the little experience of climbing.
answer: We have little experience of climbing.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-423:Bare little versus a little in an explanatory argument
explanation: Bare "little" stresses how limited the experience is. "A little" stresses the existence of some experience, which would support a more positive argument.

This highlights the experience the group does have. It does not preserve the requested emphasis on near-absence.
Bare little gives the negative orientation needed to explain the cancellation.
rationales.We have a little of the experience of cl: This awkwardly treats the experience as an identified whole with a small portion; that is not the general lack described.
rationales.We have the little experience of climbin: "The little experience" normally needs a defining continuation such as "we gained last year". It does not express the intended general shortfall here.

sentence: A website adds an unexpected fee at the final payment step. Its designer calls this 'confusing by design'. What does 'by design' mean?
setupText: Choose the meaning of the first phrase.
taskText: A website adds an unexpected fee at the final payment step. Its designer calls this 'confusing by design'. What does 'by design' mean?
text: Choose the meaning of the first phrase. A website adds an unexpected fee at the final payment step. Its designer calls this 'confusing by design'. What does 'by design' mean?
options: Confusing because the design has not yet been completed
Confusing despite a plan intended to make the process clear
Confusing in its layout rather than in the information it presents
Deliberately confusing as a planned part of the payment process
answer: Deliberately confusing as a planned part of the payment process
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-424:Zero article in the idiomatic phrase by design
explanation: By design is an article-free expression meaning intentionally. It says the confusing effect was planned, not that the design was unfinished or that only the visual layout causes difficulty.

rationales.Confusing because the design has not yet: The fixed phrase states intention. It does not attribute the confusion to unfinished work.
rationales.Deliberately confusing as a planned part: By design presents the confusing effect as deliberate, even though the phrase contains no article before design.
rationales.Confusing despite a plan intended to mak: Despite the plan would describe an unintended result. By design says the result was intended.
rationales.Confusing in its layout rather than in t: Design here is part of an idiom about intention; it does not limit the problem to visual layout.

sentence: "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the definite noun phrase.
taskText: "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
text: Choose the interpretation of the definite noun phrase. "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
options: One electric vehicle being used as the main example throughout the paragraph
The city's first electric vehicle, treated as the beginning of a wider trend
The electric vehicles in one identified fleet, rather than the vehicle type generally
Electric cars as a technological category, rather than a particular physical vehicle
answer: Electric cars as a technological category, rather than a particular physical vehicle
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-425:Generic definite singular for a technological category
explanation: A definite singular can represent a class or invention. In this general discussion, "the electric car" means the technology or vehicle type, not one physical car.

rationales.One electric vehicle being used as the m: An individual-car reading would need an identifiable vehicle. The statement about transport trends instead presents the vehicle type as an influence on cities.
rationales.Electric cars as a technological categor: The definite singular can stand for a class or technological development in a general statement.
rationales.The city's first electric vehicle, treat: The article does not give the car a first-in-history meaning; that would need wording such as the first electric car.
rationales.The electric vehicles in one identified: No fleet is identified. The category reading fits the broad claim about how cities plan their networks.

sentence: Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article change.
taskText: Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
text: Choose the interpretation of the article change. Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
options: It says her practical knowledge is greater than that of other nurses
It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
It identifies an event that the listener has already heard about
It says the event was unusual or dangerous
answer: It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-426:Experience as knowledge versus an experience as an event
explanation: Uncountable "experience" can mean accumulated knowledge. "An experience" counts one event someone went through. The article itself does not tell us whether that event was unusual, dangerous, or already known.

rationales.It presents one event she lived through: This captures the change from practical knowledge to a countable episode.
rationales.It says her practical knowledge is great: The article changes the noun's sense; it does not compare anyone's expertise.
rationales.It identifies an event that the listener: The indefinite article does not itself mark a previously identified event.
rationales.It says the event was unusual or dangero: Those qualities would need additional wording; they do not follow from "an".

sentence: 'Four volunteers left at six. ___ stayed to finish packing.' Which phrase makes the intended reference explicit?
setupText: A coordinator wants to say that every remaining volunteer stayed, not just an unspecified further group.
taskText: 'Four volunteers left at six. ___ stayed to finish packing.' Which phrase makes the intended reference explicit?
text: A coordinator wants to say that every remaining volunteer stayed, not just an unspecified further group. 'Four volunteers left at six. ___ stayed to finish packing.' Which phrase makes the intended reference explicit?
options: Other volunteers
Some other volunteers
The other volunteers
A few other volunteers
answer: The other volunteers
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-427:Definite plural remainder versus an unspecified additional group
explanation: The other volunteers identifies the remainder of the relevant volunteer group after the four who left are excluded. Bare other volunteers introduces further volunteers without explicitly presenting that complete remainder.

rationales.Other volunteers: This says that further volunteers stayed. It does not explicitly identify them as the full remainder of the group.
rationales.Some other volunteers: Some presents an unspecified portion or number. It leaves open whether additional volunteers also left.
rationales.The other volunteers: The definite plural picks out the remaining members of the already established group.
rationales.A few other volunteers: A few adds a small-number claim and does not express that every remaining member stayed.

sentence: An old resident says, 'The village has changed beyond recognition.'
setupText: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the force of the article-free expression.
taskText: An old resident says, 'The village has changed beyond recognition.'
text: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the force of the article-free expression. An old resident says, 'The village has changed beyond recognition.'
options: The village is so different that its former appearance is hard to recognise.
The village has changed in ways that few people have officially acknowledged.
The village has changed, though its old appearance remains easy to recognise.
The village has become better known because people have praised its improvements.
answer: The village is so different that its former appearance is hard to recognise.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-428:Zero article in beyond recognition
explanation: Beyond recognition means changed so much that the former appearance is hard to recognise. Recognition has no article in this fixed expression; it concerns recognising the place, not acknowledging or praising the changes.

rationales.The village has changed in ways that few: This uses recognition in the sense of acknowledgment. The resident is describing how different the village looks, not whether officials acknowledge the changes.
rationales.The village is so different that its for: The paraphrase keeps the strong degree of change expressed by beyond recognition.
rationales.The village has changed, though its old: Easy to recognise weakens and reverses the idiom's central point: the changes have made recognition difficult.
rationales.The village has become better known beca: This treats recognition as public appreciation. The phrase does not say the changes brought fame or were improvements.

sentence: A travel writer is describing the inhabitants of France as a national group. Which sentence has that reading?
setupText: Choose the sentence that refers to the people, not their language.
taskText: A travel writer is describing the inhabitants of France as a national group. Which sentence has that reading?
text: Choose the sentence that refers to the people, not their language. A travel writer is describing the inhabitants of France as a national group. Which sentence has that reading?
options: French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French have influenced the neighbouring regions.
A French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
answer: The French have influenced the neighbouring regions.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-429:The plus nationality adjective for a collective group
explanation: "The French" can name the French people collectively and takes plural agreement. Article-free "French" commonly names the language and takes singular agreement.

rationales.French has influenced the neighbouring r: This naturally names the language, while the task specifies the people.
rationales.A French has influenced the neighbouring: To refer to one person, use a countable person noun such as "a French person".
rationales.The French have influenced the neighbour: The definite group expression and plural verb identify the people collectively.
rationales.The French has influenced the neighbouri: For the national group of people, "the French" takes plural agreement, so use "have".

sentence: "During her sentence she was in prison. Years later she returned to the prison to give a talk." What does the added article help signal?
setupText: Choose the interpretation that fits the purpose of each visit.
taskText: "During her sentence she was in prison. Years later she returned to the prison to give a talk." What does the added article help signal?
text: Choose the interpretation that fits the purpose of each visit. "During her sentence she was in prison. Years later she returned to the prison to give a talk." What does the added article help signal?
options: It introduces an unfamiliar prison, then identifies a different one for the talk.
It contrasts time spent in prison generally with a return to prisoner status.
It contrasts imprisonment with a later visit to an identified institution.
It describes her earlier circumstances, then leaves the later destination unspecified.
answer: It contrasts imprisonment with a later visit to an identified institution.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-430:Bare institutional status versus definite institutional reference
explanation: "In prison" conventionally describes imprisonment. "The prison" identifies a particular institution; the talk establishes that the later visit is not another statement of prisoner status.

rationales.It contrasts imprisonment with a later v: Bare in prison expresses prisoner status; the definite phrase identifies the institution she later visits for a talk.
rationales.It introduces an unfamiliar prison, then: The first phrase expresses imprisonment rather than introducing an unfamiliar institution with a. The wording does not establish a change of prison.
rationales.It contrasts time spent in prison genera: The later purpose is giving a talk. The prison identifies her destination without saying that she is imprisoned again.
rationales.It describes her earlier circumstances,: The later definite article presents the destination as identifiable, not unspecified.

sentence: "The pilot was a success, although the wider programme still faced difficulties." What does "a success" mean?
setupText: A charity tested a new service in one town before expanding it. Choose the interpretation of the indefinite noun phrase.
taskText: "The pilot was a success, although the wider programme still faced difficulties." What does "a success" mean?
text: A charity tested a new service in one town before expanding it. Choose the interpretation of the indefinite noun phrase. "The pilot was a success, although the wider programme still faced difficulties." What does "a success" mean?
options: Success as an abstract quality of every part of the programme
The only successful activity in the organisation's history
A successful person appointed to manage the programme
One undertaking judged to have achieved a good result
answer: One undertaking judged to have achieved a good result
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-431:A success as a countable evaluative classification
explanation: "A success" classifies the pilot as a successful undertaking. It is a countable result use, whereas article-free "success" can name the abstract idea.

rationales.Success as an abstract quality of every: The article makes the pilot a countable example of success; the following clause explicitly limits the wider conclusion.
rationales.One undertaking judged to have achieved: This captures the predicative countable use in "was a success".
rationales.The only successful activity in the orga: The indefinite article classifies one case; it does not make an only-ever claim.
rationales.A successful person appointed to manage: The subject is the pilot undertaking, not a person.

sentence: "We need evidence before deciding. The evidence from yesterday's inspection is particularly relevant." Why can the second sentence use "the"?
setupText: Choose the explanation of the two article patterns.
taskText: "We need evidence before deciding. The evidence from yesterday's inspection is particularly relevant." Why can the second sentence use "the"?
text: Choose the explanation of the two article patterns. "We need evidence before deciding. The evidence from yesterday's inspection is particularly relevant." Why can the second sentence use "the"?
options: The source phrase identifies a particular body of evidence
Evidence becomes a singular count noun because it comes from one inspection
Repeating evidence requires the even if the second sentence concerns a different source
The article presents the inspection findings as conclusive rather than merely relevant
answer: The source phrase identifies a particular body of evidence
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-432:Definite reference to a specified body of uncountable evidence
explanation: The first sentence requests evidence without identifying a body of it. The second points to evidence from a specified inspection. An uncountable noun can take "the" when its reference is identifiable.

rationales.Evidence becomes a singular count noun b: Evidence remains uncountable. One identifiable source does not turn it into a count noun.
rationales.The source phrase identifies a particula: The inspection makes this evidence identifiable; an uncountable noun can take the for that purpose.
rationales.Repeating evidence requires the even if: Word repetition alone does not require the. Here the source phrase identifies which evidence the writer means.
rationales.The article presents the inspection find: Definiteness identifies the evidence; it does not increase its strength. The sentence describes it as particularly relevant, not conclusive.

sentence: Meals are excluded. Which sentence states the intended reimbursement policy?
setupText: Choose the policy wording that covers travel costs as a general category, not a named journey or a fixed allowance.
taskText: Meals are excluded. Which sentence states the intended reimbursement policy?
text: Choose the policy wording that covers travel costs as a general category, not a named journey or a fixed allowance. Meals are excluded. Which sentence states the intended reimbursement policy?
options: The company reimburses travel, but not meals.
The company reimburses the journey described above, but not meals.
The company pays a travel allowance, but not a meal allowance.
The company reimburses a return journey, but not meals.
answer: The company reimburses travel, but not meals.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-433:Editing bare expense categories versus identified journeys and countable allowances
explanation: Bare travel names the general expense category, parallel to bare plural meals. A journey counts a trip; the journey identifies one; a travel allowance names a payment arrangement rather than reimbursement of travel costs generally.

rationales.The company reimburses travel, but not m: The two article-free nouns name categories of expenses, preserving the intended general policy.
rationales.The company reimburses the journey descr: The definite phrase limits reimbursement to an identified journey rather than the general category.
rationales.The company pays a travel allowance, but: The articles introduce countable allowances. An allowance can be a fixed payment and does not state the intended reimbursement policy.
rationales.The company reimburses a return journey,: This counts one return trip and narrows the kind of journey, neither of which is part of the intended general wording.

sentence: "An essay can explore a question without answering it; the essay you submitted does neither." How do the articles guide the reader?
setupText: Choose the explanation that preserves the contrast.
taskText: "An essay can explore a question without answering it; the essay you submitted does neither." How do the articles guide the reader?
text: Choose the explanation that preserves the contrast. "An essay can explore a question without answering it; the essay you submitted does neither." How do the articles guide the reader?
options: Both phrases refer to the submitted text, first as new information and then as known information
The first identifies a model essay already written; the second identifies a student's response to it
The first introduces an unidentified text that the writer later discovers to be the submitted essay
A general possibility for essays is contrasted with an assessment of one identifiable submission
answer: A general possibility for essays is contrasted with an assessment of one identifiable submission
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-434:Generic indefinite followed by a definite individual application
explanation: "An essay" supports a general claim through a representative example. "The essay you submitted" then singles out an identifiable text for criticism.

rationales.A general possibility for essays is cont: An essay represents a class member in the general statement; the essay you submitted then identifies the particular work being assessed.
rationales.Both phrases refer to the submitted text: The first clause describes what essays can do in general. It does not introduce the submitted essay as a particular new referent.
rationales.The first identifies a model essay alrea: No existing model or response to a model is introduced. The first noun phrase supports a general possibility.
rationales.The first introduces an unidentified tex: The passage moves from generalisation to assessment, not from ignorance to discovery of a text's identity.

sentence: "There is a reason for the delay, but I cannot discuss it yet." What does "a reason" establish?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite phrase.
taskText: "There is a reason for the delay, but I cannot discuss it yet." What does "a reason" establish?
text: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite phrase. "There is a reason for the delay, but I cannot discuss it yet." What does "a reason" establish?
options: The speaker says the listener already knows the explanation
The speaker presents an explanation as existing without identifying it to the listener
The speaker guarantees that only one contributing factor exists
The speaker says the delay has no explanation that could be expressed
answer: The speaker presents an explanation as existing without identifying it to the listener
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-435:Indefinite introduction despite speaker knowledge
explanation: The indefinite article introduces a reason while withholding its identity. It does not mean the speaker is ignorant of it, nor does it prove there is only one contributing factor.

rationales.The speaker presents an explanation as e: This separates introducing a referent from revealing which one it is.
rationales.The speaker says the listener already kn: The phrase does not mark the reason as already identifiable to the listener.
rationales.The speaker guarantees that only one con: "A reason" introduces one reason; it does not exclude further reasons.
rationales.The speaker says the delay has no explan: The opening explicitly asserts that a reason exists. The speaker is declining to discuss it.

sentence: The memo cancels the concert because the venue is unsafe. We can dispute ___ without denying that repairs are needed.
setupText: Choose the phrase that identifies the previously stated reason.
taskText: The memo cancels the concert because the venue is unsafe. We can dispute ___ without denying that repairs are needed.
text: Choose the phrase that identifies the previously stated reason. The memo cancels the concert because the venue is unsafe. We can dispute ___ without denying that repairs are needed.
options: a further reason given in the memo
some other reasons given in the memo
the reason given in the memo
another reason given in the memo
answer: the reason given in the memo
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-436:Definite reference to a reason expressed as a whole proposition
explanation: The earlier sentence has supplied the reason being discussed: the venue is unsafe. "The reason given in the memo" points back to that identified reason.

rationales.a further reason given in the memo: Further adds another reason instead of pointing back to the safety reason just stated.
rationales.the reason given in the memo: The definite phrase identifies the safety justification already supplied for cancelling the concert.
rationales.some other reasons given in the memo: This introduces several different reasons; the prompt asks for the one already stated.
rationales.another reason given in the memo: Another shifts to a different reason instead of maintaining reference to the safety justification.

sentence: "After the interview, she felt a confidence she had never felt before." Why is "a confidence" possible?
setupText: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
taskText: "After the interview, she felt a confidence she had never felt before." Why is "a confidence" possible?
text: Choose the meaning of the article phrase. "After the interview, she felt a confidence she had never felt before." Why is "a confidence" possible?
options: It counts one secret she has told the interviewer
It presents a particular kind or instance of the feeling, described by the following clause
It identifies the feeling as already shared by all the interviewers
It means the noun confidence is always countable after felt
answer: It presents a particular kind or instance of the feeling, described by the following clause
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-437:A characterised manifestation of an abstract feeling
explanation: An abstract feeling can be presented as a particular manifestation when it is characterised: "a confidence she had never felt before". This does not make every use of confidence countable.

rationales.It presents a particular kind or instanc: The following clause characterises the distinctive confidence she experienced.
rationales.It counts one secret she has told the in: "A confidence" can mean a secret in other contexts, but "felt" and the repeated feeling point to self-assurance.
rationales.It identifies the feeling as already sha: The sentence concerns her feeling and does not establish a shared state among interviewers.
rationales.It means the noun confidence is always c: Compare "She felt confidence in the plan". Countability depends on the chosen interpretation, not a universal rule after felt.

sentence: "The dentist offered an appointment on Friday. Unfortunately, the time clashes with my shift." How does the listener identify "the time"?
setupText: Choose the explanation of the definite reference.
taskText: "The dentist offered an appointment on Friday. Unfortunately, the time clashes with my shift." How does the listener identify "the time"?
text: Choose the explanation of the definite reference. "The dentist offered an appointment on Friday. Unfortunately, the time clashes with my shift." How does the listener identify "the time"?
options: As the time associated with the offered appointment
As every available appointment time on Friday
As the current clock time during the conversation
As a new unspecified time that the dentist has not offered
answer: As the time associated with the offered appointment
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-438:Associated definite reference to an appointment's time
explanation: An appointment conventionally has a scheduled time. The offered appointment therefore makes "the time" identifiable without a previous literal mention of the word time.

rationales.As the time associated with the offered: The relationship between an appointment and its time supplies the reference.
rationales.As every available appointment time on F: The singular phrase refers to the offered appointment's time, not all available slots.
rationales.As the current clock time during the con: The clash is with a shift at the appointment time, not with the moment of speaking.
rationales.As a new unspecified time that the denti: The definite phrase depends on the appointment just offered; it does not introduce an unrelated time.

sentence: The speaker means people who are out of work as a group. Which sentence expresses that?
setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence for this meaning.
taskText: The speaker means people who are out of work as a group. Which sentence expresses that?
text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence for this meaning. The speaker means people who are out of work as a group. Which sentence expresses that?
options: An unemployed needs access to affordable training.
The unemployeds need access to affordable training.
An unemployed people need access to affordable training.
The unemployed need access to affordable training.
answer: The unemployed need access to affordable training.
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-439:The plus adjective forming a collective human group
explanation: "The unemployed" uses the adjective to refer collectively to unemployed people. It takes plural agreement but does not add a plural -s to the adjective.

rationales.The unemployed need access to affordable: The definite article plus adjective names the group, with the plural verb "need".
rationales.An unemployed needs access to affordable: To count one person, say "an unemployed person"; unemployed does not normally stand as that singular count noun.
rationales.The unemployeds need access to affordabl: Do not add plural -s to the adjective in this group construction.
rationales.An unemployed people need access to affo: The singular article "an" cannot introduce plural "people".

sentence: "The campaign gave the issue publicity, though not the publicity the organisers wanted." What does the second phrase do?
setupText: Choose the interpretation of the repeated noun.
taskText: "The campaign gave the issue publicity, though not the publicity the organisers wanted." What does the second phrase do?
text: Choose the interpretation of the repeated noun. "The campaign gave the issue publicity, though not the publicity the organisers wanted." What does the second phrase do?
options: It counts one advertisement purchased by the organisers
It identifies a desired kind of public attention and contrasts it with the attention received
It states that the campaign received no public attention
It establishes that all publicity was arranged in advance
answer: It identifies a desired kind of public attention and contrasts it with the attention received
focusKey: coverage-articles-b2-440:Definite reference to a desired kind of an uncountable phenomenon
explanation: The first article-free use names public attention generally. "The publicity the organisers wanted" then identifies the particular kind or character of attention they had hoped for.

rationales.It counts one advertisement purchased by: "Publicity" remains uncountable; the sentence does not identify a purchased advertisement.
rationales.It identifies a desired kind of public a: This preserves both the existence of publicity and the qualification about its character.
rationales.It states that the campaign received no: The first clause explicitly says the issue received publicity.
rationales.It establishes that all publicity was ar: Wanting a kind of attention does not mean the actual attention was planned or controlled.
